He painted the farms, rivers, and clouds of the countryside he grew up in, often outdoors, which was unusual at the time. He lived in London for much of his adult life. He was more admired in France than at home, and his work inspired the Barbizon painters and Impressionists.

Q1009816.bio: Gerhard Munthe was a Norwegian painter and designer, born in 1849. He was a leader in reviving Norwegian folk art and illustrated Norse sagas. His bright, decorative style influenced Norwegian design. He died in Lysaker in 1929.

Q45006.bio: Franz von Stuck was born in Bavaria, Germany, and became a celebrated painter and teacher in Munich. He was a founding member of the Munich Secession and painted mysterious and powerful symbolic pictures. Kandinsky and Klee were among his students. He lived in a grand villa in Munich, which is now a museum.

Q212754.bio: John William Waterhouse was born in Rome to English parents and later lived in London. He painted women from myths and legends — such as the Lady of Shalott and sirens — in lush, colorful detail. He admired the Pre-Raphaelites, who came before him. He died in London in 1917.

x-league-of-women-voters.bio: The League of Women Voters was founded in 1920 by suffragist Carrie Chapman Catt, as women across the United States won the right to vote. The organization still teaches people about voting and publishes posters and guides.

Q235903.bio: Evelyn De Morgan was born in London and studied at the Slade School of Art. She was a Pre-Raphaelite painter who painted glowing allegories about peace, war and the spirit. She lived in London and Florence and was also a pacifist and a supporter of women's rights. She died in 1919.

Q263080.bio: Hugo Simberg was born in Hamina, Finland, and studied art in Helsinki and Paris. He lived mainly in Finland and painted strange, gentle scenes full of angels, devils, and skeletons, often with a wink of humor. His work blends Finnish folk tales with Symbolism. He died in 1917 at age 43.

Q2132490.bio: Loyset Liédet was a manuscript painter born in Hesdin around 1420. He worked for the Dukes of Burgundy in Bruges, painting large histories and chronicles in miniature for their libraries. He died in Bruges in 1479.

Q1659496.bio: Kamal-ol-Molk was born in Kashan, Iran, in 1848 and became the court painter of the Qajar kings. He studied European painting and painted portraits and scenes of daily life with great realism. He later founded an art school in Tehran. He died in Nishapur in 1940.

Q155626.bio: John Singer Sargent was born in Florence, Italy, to American parents and grew up traveling around Europe. He trained in Paris, then worked mostly in London, becoming the most sought-after portrait painter of his day. He painted with dazzling, confident brushwork and also made lovely watercolors on trips to Venice and the Alps. During World War I he painted soldiers at the front. He died in London in 1925.

Q76829.bio: Alexander Ivanov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and spent nearly 20 years in Rome working on one giant painting, 'The Appearance of Christ to the People'. He made hundreds of studies for it. He returned to Russia shortly before his death in 1858. His art deeply influenced Russian painters.

Q229272.bio: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner was born in Aschaffenburg, Germany, and trained as an architect before he became a founder of the group Die Brücke ('The Bridge'). He lived in Dresden and Berlin and later in the Swiss Alps near Davos. His jagged, colorful paintings made him a star of German Expressionism. He died in Switzerland in 1938.

Q69651.bio: Eduard Bendemann was born in Berlin to a Jewish family and became one of Germany's leading painters. He studied in Berlin and then worked in Dresden and Düsseldorf, where he became the director of the art academy. His paintings of Bible stories and everyday life were admired all over Europe. He died in Düsseldorf in 1889.

Q112894782.bio: Yosef Zvi Geiger was a painter from Safed, in the Holy Land under Ottoman rule. He painted religious scenes and local life in a simple, heartfelt style. He lived and worked in Safed, a town famous for Jewish study. He is remembered as one of the earliest painters from the land of Israel.

Q364226.bio: Kuzma Petrov-Vodkin was born in a small town on the Volga River in Russia, and trained in Moscow, Saint Petersburg, and Paris. He used Russian icon painting as inspiration for his bold, simple style. He later taught in Saint Petersburg (then Leningrad). He died there in 1939.

Q356644.bio: Albert Edelfelt was born in Finland to a Swedish family and studied in Antwerp and Paris. He painted portraits, scenes of Finnish life, and historical subjects. He was one of the most famous Finnish painters. He died in Finland in 1905.

Q436803.bio: Hanna Hirsch-Pauli was born in Stockholm in 1864 and was a leading Swedish woman painter. She studied in Stockholm and Paris and was a friend of many Nordic painters. She is best known for her warm family scenes. She died in 1940.

Q701669.bio: Hans Gude was born in Christiania (Oslo), Norway, and spent much of his career in Germany. He was a star of Norwegian landscape painting, depicting mountains, fjords and coasts. He taught in Düsseldorf and Berlin and trained many painters. He died in Berlin in 1903.

Q506000.bio: Paul Kane was born in Ireland and grew up in Toronto. Between 1845 and 1848 he made a long journey across Canada to the Pacific, sketching Indigenous peoples and landscapes. He then painted a series of large pictures from his sketches. He died in Toronto in 1871.

Q11977827.bio: Jacob Bratland was a Norwegian painter born in Bergen in 1859. He studied in Germany and painted landscapes of western Norway. He died in Christiania in 1906.

Q160252.bio: Frederic Leighton was born in Scarborough, England, and traveled across Europe as a child, speaking several languages. He became a leading Victorian painter of classical subjects and was President of the Royal Academy. He was the first British artist to be made a baron. His house in London is now a museum.

Q216873.bio: Pierre Puvis de Chavannes was a French painter born in Lyon in 1824. He painted calm, pale murals for the Panthéon in Paris and other public buildings, in a style that influenced many later artists. He died in Paris in 1898.

Q2339347.bio: Ivan Grohar was born in what is now Slovenia and became one of the country's best-known painters. He painted farmers and landscapes in bright, bold colors. He studied in Ljubljana and Munich. He died in Ljubljana in 1911.

x-leonardo-da-vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was born in the village of Vinci, near Florence, in 1452. He painted the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, but he was also a scientist, engineer and inventor who filled notebooks with ideas for flying machines and anatomy. He worked in Florence, Milan, Rome and France, where he died in 1519.

x-unknown-photographer.bio: The photographer who made this picture is not known. Press photographers and news agencies of the early 1900s often did not record the names of the people who took their photographs.

Q15104963.bio: Julian Russell Story was an American painter born in Walton-on-Thames, England, in 1857. He was the son of the sculptor William Wetmore Story, studied in Paris, and later lived in Philadelphia, where he died in 1919.

Q7724.bio: August Strindberg was born in Stockholm, Sweden, and is best known as one of the world's greatest playwrights and novelists. He also painted dramatic, stormy landscapes in his later years, which were far ahead of their time. He lived in Sweden, Germany, France and Denmark. He died in Stockholm in 1912.

Q295144.bio: Gustave Caillebotte was born into a wealthy Paris family and trained as a lawyer and engineer before painting. He was an Impressionist, but his pictures often show unusual high or low perspectives of the modern city. He generously used his money to support his friends, buying their paintings. He lived near Paris and died in Gennevilliers at 45.

Q662983.bio: Theodoros Vryzakis was a Greek painter born in Thebes in 1814. He studied in Munich and became known for large paintings of the Greek War of Independence, which helped shape Greek national memory. He died in Munich in 1878.

Q1555416.bio: Gustaf Cederström was born in Stockholm in 1845 and was a Swedish painter known for dramatic history paintings. He studied in Düsseldorf and Paris. He later became director of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. He died in 1933.

Q3114975.bio: Gustav Wentzel was born in Christiania in 1859 and became a Norwegian painter of everyday scenes and portraits. He studied in Paris and Munich and lived later in Lillehammer. His honest interiors were praised. He died in 1927.

Q318427.bio: Mikhail Nesterov was born in Ufa, Russia, and became a leading painter of religious and spiritual scenes. He painted frescoes in churches and created poetic pictures of saints in Russian landscapes. He lived through the Russian Revolution and continued painting in Moscow. He died there in 1942.

Q643303.bio: Jules Girardet was a French painter born in Paris in 1856, from a family of artists. He painted scenes of war and the French colonial empire, and illustrated books and magazines. He died in Boulogne-Billancourt in 1938.

Q8017370.bio: William Ranney was an American painter born in Middletown, Connecticut, in 1813. He fought in the Texas Revolution as a young man and painted scenes of the American West and of the Revolutionary War. He lived in New Jersey and died in West Hoboken in 1857.

Q3130641.bio: Henri Beau was born in Montreal and studied in Paris, where he spent much of his life. He painted historical scenes of Canada and later official war paintings. He died in Paris in 1949.

Q1390711.bio: Kolë Idromeno was born in Shkodër, Albania, and became a painter, architect and sculptor. He studied in Italy and is regarded as a pioneer of modern Albanian art. He designed buildings in his hometown. He died in Shkodër in 1939.

Q5589.bio: Henri Matisse was born in northern France and began painting after an illness at age 20. He lived in Paris and then in Nice in the south, where he painted in bold, free colors. He was the leader of Fauvism, whose name means 'wild beasts', and later made colorful paper cut-outs. He died in Nice in 1954.

Q187850.bio: Mathew Brady was an American photographer born in New York State in 1822. He ran studios in New York and Washington, photographed presidents, and organized teams of photographers who recorded the Civil War. He died in New York City in 1896.

Q167220.bio: Cornelis Cort was a Dutch engraver born in Hoorn in 1533. He moved to Venice and then Rome, where he made prints after famous paintings by Titian, Raphael and others, spreading their compositions across Europe. He died in Rome around 1575.

Q11534323.bio: Ryūsai Shigeharu was a Japanese printmaker who worked in Osaka in the early 1800s. He made woodblock prints of kabuki actors and scenes of the theater. Fans bought these prints to remember their favorite performers.

Q1190012.bio: Osman Hamdi Bey was born in Istanbul, in the Ottoman Empire, and studied painting in Paris. He was also an archaeologist and founded Istanbul's first modern art school and archaeological museum. His paintings show scenes of Ottoman life with great detail. He died in 1910 and is honored as a pioneer of Turkish art.

Q194402.bio: Joshua Reynolds was born in Plympton, England, and became the first president of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. He was the most famous portrait painter of Britain in the 1700s, and he painted kings, writers, and children. He gave important lectures about art and was knighted. He died in London in 1792.

Q762949.bio: August Malmström was born in Sweden and became a painter of Nordic legends, fairy tales and landscapes. He studied in Stockholm and Düsseldorf. He later directed the Swedish National Museum's art school. He died in Stockholm in 1901.

Q4215366.bio: James Wilson Carmichael was an English painter born in Newcastle upon Tyne in 1799. He started as a sailor and became a well-known painter of ships, sea battles and harbor scenes, and moved to London. He died in Scarborough in 1868.

Q724148.bio: Édouard Detaille was a French painter born in Paris in 1848. He studied with Meissonier and became the most celebrated painter of the French army, making huge, accurate pictures of the war of 1870 and of Napoleon's troops. He lived in Paris and died there in 1912.

x-illustrator-b-h.bio: This print was made by an illustrator who signed it with the initials B&H. Prints like this appeared in magazines and books to show readers far away what the West looked like.

Q964791.bio: Paul Émile Chabas was born in Nantes, France, and became a popular painter in Paris. He is best known for dreamy paintings of young people by lakes and meadows in soft light. His work was admired by the public in the early 1900s. He died in Paris in 1937.

Q216406.bio: Edward Burne-Jones was born in Birmingham, England, and moved to London to become an artist. He was part of the second wave of Pre-Raphaelites and also designed stained glass and tapestries with William Morris. His dreamy paintings were inspired by medieval legends and myths. He was made a baronet and died in London in 1898.

Q2666703.bio: Halfdan Egedius was born in Drammen in 1877 and became one of the most promising Norwegian painters of his generation, especially for his landscapes and book illustrations. He died of illness at the age of 22, in 1899.

x-nasa-photograph-by-neil-armstrong.bio: Neil Armstrong, born in 1930 in Ohio, was the commander of Apollo 11 and the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969. Because he carried the camera, most of the famous photographs from the Moon walk show Buzz Aldrin, not him. He died in 2012.

Q3106117.bio: Lawren Harris was born in Brantford, Ontario, and was a founding member of the Group of Seven. He became known for his bold, simple paintings of Lake Superior, the Rocky Mountains and the Arctic. His work shaped the idea of the Canadian landscape. He died in Vancouver in 1970.

Q786545.bio: Thomas Sully was an English-born American painter born in Horncastle in 1783. He moved to America as a boy, settled in Philadelphia and painted portraits of many leaders, including Queen Victoria. He died in Philadelphia in 1872.

Q123071.bio: Arnold Böcklin was born in Basel, Switzerland, and spent long periods in Italy and Germany. He painted dreamy scenes full of myths, strange creatures and mysterious islands. He is best known for 'Isle of the Dead'. He died near Florence in 1901.

x-johannes-vingboons.bio: Johannes Vingboons was a Dutch mapmaker and painter born in Amsterdam around 1616. He drew maps and views of the world for the Dutch West India Company, including early views of New Amsterdam, now New York. He lived in Amsterdam and died there around 1670.

Q718795.bio: Vincenzo Camuccini was born in Rome and became one of Italy's leading Neoclassical painters. He painted big history scenes and was in charge of the Vatican's paintings. He was also a collector. He died in Rome in 1844.

Q3319624.bio: Molly Bobak was a Canadian painter born in Vancouver in 1920. She was the first woman official war artist in the Canadian army in World War II, married the artist Bruno Bobak, and lived in Fredericton, New Brunswick, until she died in 2014.

Q181568.bio: Ivan Aivazovsky was born in Feodosia, a port town on the Crimean coast of the Black Sea. He became one of the greatest painters of the sea, producing about 6,000 works in his career. He traveled widely in Europe and served as a Russian navy painter. He lived most of his life in Feodosia, where he built a studio and art gallery for his hometown.

Q445891.bio: Frits Thaulow was born in Christiania (Oslo) and became a leading Norwegian Impressionist, known for painting water in rivers, streams and mills. He lived in France and Denmark, as well as in Norway. He died in 1906.

Q150679.bio: Anthony van Dyck was a Flemish painter born in Antwerp in 1599. He was Rubens's most gifted assistant, traveled to Italy, and in 1632 moved to London as court painter to King Charles I, where he set the style for English portraits. He died in London in 1641 at the age of 42.

Q1513704.bio: Gerlach Flicke was a German painter born in Osnabrück around 1495. He moved to England, where he lived in London and painted portraits, including one of Archbishop Thomas Cranmer. He died in London in 1558.

Q1441554.bio: Francis Hayman was an English painter born in Exeter in 1708. He worked in London, painting scenes for the pleasure gardens at Vauxhall and large history pictures, and was one of the founders of the Royal Academy. He died in London in 1776.

x-anonymous-kurz-allison.bio: Kurz and Allison was an American printing firm in Chicago that made colorful lithographs of famous battles and historical scenes in the 1880s and 1890s. Their prints brought the Civil War and the American West into many homes.

Q122382.bio: Henry Fuseli was born in Zurich, Switzerland, and moved to England as a young man. He became a professor at the Royal Academy in London. He loved stories of ghosts, witches, and nightmares and painted them with dramatic, wild imagination. His artwork influenced the Romantic movement and later the Surrealists.

Q6141349.bio: James Pollock was an American artist who served in the US Army's combat art program in Vietnam in 1967. His paintings of the war and the jungle are part of the Army's art collection.

Q374744.bio: Kanō Naizen was a Japanese painter born in 1570 who belonged to the Kanō school, the main painting school of the Japanese military rulers. He lived in Kyoto and is known for his colorful folding screens of the Portuguese traders who arrived in Japan. He died in Kyoto in 1616.

Q514628.bio: Russell Lee was an American photographer born in Ottawa, Illinois, in 1903. He worked for the Farm Security Administration, took thousands of pictures of rural life in the 1930s and 1940s, and later taught photography in Texas. He died in Austin in 1986.

Q17627030.bio: Robert Herdman was a Scottish painter born in Rattray in Perthshire in 1829. He lived in Edinburgh and painted scenes from Scottish history and everyday life, and became a leading member of the Royal Scottish Academy. He died in Edinburgh in 1888.

Q63596.bio: Carl Gustaf Hellqvist was born in Sweden in 1851 and studied in Stockholm and Munich. He painted large history paintings full of drama. He died young, in Munich, at 39.

Q450490.bio: Bernt Notke was a German painter and sculptor born in the Baltic region around 1440. He worked in Lübeck, Tallinn and Stockholm, and made big works for churches, including the Danse Macabre in Tallinn. He died in Lübeck in 1509.

Q539474.bio: Constantin Hansen was born in Rome to Danish parents and grew up in Copenhagen. He was a leading painter of the Danish Golden Age and painted portraits, historical scenes and murals. He also visited Italy. He died near Copenhagen in 1880.

Q391608.bio: Asher Brown Durand was born in New Jersey and began as an engraver before becoming a landscape painter. He was a leader of the Hudson River School and the second president of the National Academy of Design. His painting 'Kindred Spirits' is a famous American image. He died in 1886.

Q159606.bio: John Everett Millais was born in Southampton, England, and was a child prodigy who entered the Royal Academy at 11. He co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a group that painted with bright color and fine detail. Later he became a famous society painter and was made a baronet, the first artist to receive that honor. He ended his life as President of the Royal Academy in London.

Q379300.bio: Giovanni Segantini was born in Arco, in the Alps, and became a leading Italian painter of mountain scenes. He lived in the Swiss Alps, painting glowing, detailed landscapes and shepherds. He died at the age of 41 on a mountain peak, in 1899.

Q8010746.bio: William Halsall was an English-born American painter, born in Kirkdale near Liverpool in 1841. He moved to Boston and painted ships and the sea, including the Mayflower, and had a studio in the city. He died in Winthrop, Massachusetts, in 1919.

Q123098.bio: Angelica Kauffman was born in Chur, Switzerland, and was a child prodigy who traveled across Europe as a teen artist. She lived in Italy and London, where she became a founding member of the Royal Academy of Arts. She painted portraits and scenes from myth and history. She died in Rome in 1807.

Q82445.bio: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was born into a noble family in Albi, France, but broken bones in childhood stunted his growth. He moved to Montmartre in Paris and painted the dancers, singers and cabaret stars of the Moulin Rouge. His bold posters helped invent modern advertising art. He died at 36, at his mother's château in southwestern France.

Q203828.bio: Gustave Moreau was born in Paris and became a leading Symbolist painter. He painted glittering scenes from myth and the Bible, with fantastic detail. He later taught at the École des Beaux-Arts, where Matisse was a student. His Paris house is now a museum.

Q711770.bio: Dirck van Delen was a Dutch painter born in Heusden in 1605. He specialized in imaginary views of church and palace interiors, and lived for most of his life in Arnemuiden and Middelburg in Zeeland. He died in Middelburg in 1671.

Q2149073.bio: Victor Honoré Janssens was a Flemish painter born in Brussels in 1658. He painted historical, mythological and religious pictures for churches and nobles in Brussels, where he lived and worked until he died in 1736.

paintings.why: A giant wave curls over like a claw above three small fishing boats, with Mount Fuji tiny and calm in the distance. Katsushika Hokusai made this woodblock print around 1831 when he was about 70, and it became the most famous image of Japanese art in the world. Thousands of copies were printed, and it inspired artists in Europe like Van Gogh and Monet. It's a perfect picture of nature's power.
paintings.k: Count the three boats, then spot tiny Mount Fuji hiding under the wave. What do the wave's foamy fingertips look like?

paintings.why: Van Gogh painted this from memory while staying in a hospital in southern France, and the swirling sky seems to be alive with energy. Instead of copying what he saw, he painted how the night felt: glowing stars, a rolling wind and a sleepy village below. The bold, curling brushstrokes were revolutionary, and they showed artists they could paint emotions, not just objects. Today it is one of the most recognized paintings on Earth.
paintings.k: Count the glowing stars in the sky, then find the tall church steeple in the village below.

paintings.why: A woman holding the French flag charges over a barricade, with people of every background following her. Delacroix painted it after the 1830 July Revolution in Paris, and it turned a real uprising into a symbol of freedom. The drama, color and movement made it a landmark of Romantic painting. Its image of Liberty has inspired posters, stamps, and even the Statue of Liberty's story.

Mount Fuji glows red in the morning sun, with white clouds drifting and a deep blue sky. Hokusai made this woodblock print, called 'Red Fuji,' as part of his series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. The mountain looks big and calm, like a friendly giant. It's one of the most beloved prints from Japan.
paintings.k: Mount Fuji glows red in the morning. What color is the sky?

paintings.why: Van Gogh wanted to show how poor farmers really lived, so he painted a family sharing a humble meal of potatoes by lamplight. The dark, earthy colors and rough faces were deliberate: he wanted to honor honest work with hands that dug the food they ate. It was his first big masterpiece, painted long before his famous bright colors. It reminds us that great art can be about ordinary, hardworking people.

Monet painted the misty port of Le Havre at dawn, with a small orange sun and boats made of just a few quick strokes. When critics saw it in 1874, one mockingly said it was only an 'impression' — and the name Impressionism was born! The painting captures a fleeting moment of light instead of fine details. It launched a whole movement that changed how people think about painting.

The ancient Greek thinker Socrates was sentenced to drink poison, and David shows him calmly raising a finger to make one last point while friends weep around him. The clear, sculpture-like figures and calm lighting made it a model of Neoclassical painting. It is famous because it makes a big idea — standing up for your beliefs, even at great cost — feel real and powerful.

Two lovers are wrapped together in a golden robe, covered in glittering patterns, kneeling on a flower-dotted meadow. Klimt used real gold leaf, which makes the painting shimmer like a jewel. He mixed flat, decorative patterns with soft, realistic faces and hands. It became the most famous work of the Vienna Secession and is loved around the world as a picture of tenderness.

paintings.t: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
paintings.why: A lone traveler stands on a rocky peak with his back to us, gazing over a sea of mist and mountains. Friedrich wanted us to stand in his place and feel awe at nature's size and mystery. It has become the icon of Romanticism, the idea that nature and personal feelings matter deeply. We still know it because everyone has felt like that tiny wanderer at some big, quiet view.
paintings.k: He stands on a rock above the clouds. What would you see if you stood beside him?

paintings.why: In 1816 a French ship wrecked, and a handful of survivors drifted on a raft for almost two weeks. Géricault painted the moment they spot rescue far away, using huge, life-size figures and dramatic light. He even studied real survivors to get the details right. The painting was a sensation, turning a news story into a timeless picture of hope and survival against terrible odds.

According to legend, a band of Cossack warriors received an insulting demand from the Turkish sultan to surrender, and they responded with a joke-filled, rude letter. Repin shows them roaring with laughter as the scribe writes. It took him over a decade, and the laughing faces are so lively you can almost hear them. It's beloved in Ukraine and Russia for its humor and spirit.

Goya painted a woman reclining on a couch, looking directly at the viewer in a way that was bold and unusual for its time. The painting got him into trouble with the Spanish Inquisition, which only added to its fame. It is remembered for its honest, real-person feeling instead of the idealized goddesses artists usually painted. It's also famously paired with a clothed twin, La maja vestida.

A firing squad aims at a man in a white shirt who raises his arms, while others wait their turn in the dark. Goya painted this to remember Spanish citizens who were executed after standing up to Napoleon's army. He used a glowing lantern and a faceless line of soldiers to make the cruelty of war feel real. It's considered one of the first truly modern anti-war paintings.

Manet showed a picnic in the woods where two men in everyday suits sit with a woman who isn't dressed for the occasion — and the Paris art world was shocked. Everyone expected nudes to be goddesses from myths, not modern people at lunch. It was rejected from the official show in 1863, then displayed in the famous 'Salon of the Rejected.' It marks a turning point toward modern art.

paintings.t: Bal du moulin de la Galette
paintings.why: On a sunny Sunday in Montmartre, Parisians dance and chat under trees dappled with light. Renoir painted it on the spot with his friends as models, capturing the happiness of an ordinary afternoon. The flickering spots of sunlight on clothing are a hallmark of Impressionism. It's famous for making you feel as if you've joined the party, and it's one of the most valuable paintings ever sold.

A woman reclines on a bed, looking straight at us, with a maid bringing flowers and a black cat at her feet. Manet's frank, flat style and her confident gaze scandalized visitors in 1865; some even tried to attack it. Instead of a polite myth, he painted a real modern woman who isn't shy. Today it is seen as a brave starting point of modern art.

Van Gogh painted these irises in the garden of the hospital where he was staying. The purple blooms rise and bend across a sea of green, with one lonely white flower standing out. The bold outlines were inspired by Japanese woodblock prints, which he adored. It sold for a record-setting price in 1987 and remains one of the most beloved flower paintings ever.
paintings.k: Find the one white flower among all the purple irises.

paintings.why: A golden field under a stormy blue sky, with a path that seems to run out and crows swirling overhead. Van Gogh painted it in the final weeks of his life, and many people read deep feelings of loneliness in it. Whatever he meant, the wild brushwork and bold color are unforgettable. It's often shown as the ultimate example of how painting can carry strong emotion.

Three brothers in ancient Rome stretch out their arms to swear to fight for their city, while the women of the family weep. David's sharp lines, stage-like setting and strong sense of duty were a stunning change from the frilly paintings that came before. It helped create Neoclassicism and was admired in the years before the French Revolution as a picture of courage and sacrifice.

paintings.t: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
paintings.why: People hurry across a wooden bridge in a sudden rainstorm, with sheets of rain falling in black lines, and rafts on the river below. Utagawa Hiroshige made this woodblock print in 1857, and Vincent van Gogh was so struck by it that he copied it in oil. The lines of rain and the dark clouds are dramatic. It's one of the most famous prints in Japan.
paintings.k: The rain falls in thin black lines. How many people are on the bridge?

paintings.why: Jean-Paul Marat, a French revolutionary, lies in his bathtub after being stabbed, clutching a letter in his hand. David was his friend, and he painted it like a sacred picture, with quiet light and an empty background. It's famous because it turned a news event into a haunting memorial. The painting shows how art can shape how people remember history.
l: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium

paintings.why: A warm yellow glow from a café spills onto cobblestones beneath a deep blue night sky full of stars. Van Gogh painted this in Arles, France, and it was among the first times he painted night without using black. The contrast of orange light against blue is a joy to the eye. It still makes people want to sit down and enjoy an evening there.
paintings.k: Find the stars above the cafe. Why do you think the painter didn't use any black?

paintings.why: A barmaid stands in front of a mirror at a busy Paris nightclub, looking sad and distant while the crowd sparkles behind her. Manet painted it near the end of his life, and the mirror reflection doesn't quite match what we'd expect, which still puzzles people. It captures the buzz of modern city life and the loneliness inside it. It's one of the great mysteries of art.

A young man in a shimmering blue satin suit stands proudly against a stormy landscape. Gainsborough painted it partly to prove he could use blue as a main color — something many artists of his day believed was a mistake. It became hugely famous, and in 1922 it was shipped from England to California, drawing crowds who came to say goodbye. It's a classic of British portrait painting.
l: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

paintings.why: Napoleon, in 1804, took the crown from the Pope and placed it on his own head — and then crowned his wife Josephine, which is the moment David painted. It is enormous, about 10 meters wide, and packed with 200 life-size people. David was Napoleon's official painter, and the picture was meant to show power and glory. It's still a famous record of one of history's biggest ceremonies.

A huge plum tree branch stretches across the picture in the foreground, with a garden full of blossoms in the distance. Utagawa Hiroshige made this woodblock print in 1857 as part of One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. Vincent van Gogh copied it in oil paint in 1887 and showed how much he admired Japanese art. It's a bold and beautiful print.
paintings.k: A big branch crosses the picture. What is in the distance?

paintings.why: Van Gogh painted a late-night café in Arles with clashing reds and greens and harsh lamps glowing. He said he wanted to show a place where people could 'ruin themselves, go mad or commit a crime.' The bold colors are meant to feel uneasy. It's famous as an example of how colors alone can create a mood, and it changed the way many artists used them.

Gas lamps shimmer in long golden reflections on the river as the Big Dipper glitters overhead and a couple strolls on the shore. Van Gogh painted it outdoors at night in Arles, perhaps with candles on his hat for light. It's calmer and more peaceful than his later Starry Night, and many people consider it just as beautiful. It shows his love of the night sky.
paintings.k: Look for the Big Dipper in the sky and the lights shining on the water.

paintings.why: Goya painted this dark picture of the Roman god Saturn on the wall of his own house, never meant for anyone else to see. It's based on a myth in which a king fears his children will replace him. The wild eyes and gloomy darkness make it one of the most intense images in art. It's famous because it shows how artists can explore fear and madness — be warned, it's scary!

A fisherman stands on a rock in the swirling sea with a net, as Mount Fuji rises in the distance. This woodblock print by Hokusai shows him pulling a line against the rolling waves. The simple shapes are very bold. It's part of his series of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.

Survivors of a shipwreck cling to a broken mast as a giant wave, the 'ninth wave' of sailors' legend, rises before them — but sunrise lights the sky with hope. Aivazovsky painted the sea so glowing and real that people felt the spray. He is Russia's most beloved painter of the ocean, and this canvas is his best-known work. It's famous for its drama and its message that hope returns with the dawn.
paintings.k: The sun is rising. Find the sailors and see what they're clinging to.

paintings.why: Workers in a vineyard carry baskets of grapes under a blazing orange sun, with the whole field glowing red and gold. Van Gogh painted it in Arles in 1888. For a long time it was believed to be the only painting he sold during his life, though that is now thought to be uncertain. It remains famous for its heat and bright, joyful colors.

This is the actual house in Arles, France, where Van Gogh lived and hoped to start a community of artists. He painted it with a bright blue sky and a sunny, buttery yellow — his color for happiness. Fellow painter Paul Gauguin stayed there, but the friendship went badly. It's loved as a cheerful portrait of a hopeful dream, and as a window into his life.
paintings.k: The painter lived in this house. Which window do you think was his?

paintings.why: A twisting, wavy church stands against a deep blue sky while a woman walks on a path beside it. Van Gogh painted it in 1890, just weeks before his death, and the building almost seems alive. The strong cobalt blue sky and the curving lines give ordinary architecture a dreamlike feel. It's loved because it turns a small village church into something powerful and unforgettable.

It is exactly what it sounds like: a black square on a white background. Malevich showed it in 1915 and called it a new beginning for painting, free of any picture of the real world. He wanted art to be about pure feeling and shape. People still argue about it, and that's why it is famous: it asked 'what is art?' and changed painting forever.

Eleven men, bent over and tied to ropes, drag a heavy boat up a river in the burning sun. Repin saw this hard labor himself, and he painted each man as a real person with his own story. It shocked Russian viewers who had rarely seen working people shown with such respect. It's celebrated as a masterpiece of Russian realism and a call for compassion.

paintings.t: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
paintings.why: Parisians relax by a river on a sunny Sunday — but the whole picture is made of tiny dots of pure color! Seurat spent two years on it, studying the science of how our eyes mix colors. Standing back, the dots blend into glowing light. This technique, called pointillism, was brand new. It's famous for being both a quiet picnic and a daring experiment.

paintings.t: Under the Mannen Bridge at Fukagawa
paintings.why: A water bucket hangs from a rope under a tall bridge over a canal, with Mount Fuji in the circle of the arch. Hokusai made this clever woodblock print, a view framed in a tricky way. The strong curve of the bridge is dramatic. It's a fun surprise when you spot Fuji.

A fashionable Viennese lady sits in a glimmering swirl of gold, patterns and eyes, with only her face and hands painted realistically. Klimt covered the canvas in gold leaf, like a Byzantine mosaic. During World War II the painting was taken from its owners, and decades later her family won it back in a famous legal case. Its story is as dramatic as its sparkle.

A young woman in a frothy pink dress swings high in a leafy garden while a man hides in the bushes and another gives her a push. Fragonard painted it for a rich French nobleman, and the whole thing is playful, fluffy and fun. Her shoe is flying off into the air! It's the best-known painting of the Rococo style, which celebrated lightness and delight.
paintings.k: Find the girl's shoe flying through the air! Can you spot the man hiding in the bushes?

paintings.why: A woman reclines on a couch with her back to us, looking over her shoulder. Ingres stretched her body longer than is natural, adding extra vertebrae on purpose to create a graceful curve. Critics at the time found it strange, but today it's admired for its elegant lines and silky textures. It's an important example of how artists sometimes break reality for beauty.

Courbet painted a funeral in his small hometown on a canvas as big as a history painting. The mourners are ordinary villagers, shown just as they were, without glamor. In 1850 this was shocking, since big canvases were reserved for kings and heroes. It is famous as a landmark of Realism, the idea that everyday people deserve to be painted as important.

A young woman floats in a river among flowers, singing as she drifts, based on a scene from Shakespeare's Hamlet. Millais painted every leaf and petal with incredible detail, spending months outdoors beside a river. The model, Elizabeth Siddal, lay in a bathtub filled with water for hours. It's one of the most beloved works of the Pre-Raphaelites, who loved nature and storytelling.

The Roman goddess Venus rises from the sea on a shell, surrounded by cherubs and carried to shore on the wind. Bouguereau painted her with a smooth, porcelain finish popular in the French Salon. It was a huge hit when new and made him one of the most famous painters in the world. It's a showpiece of academic painting.

paintings.t: Ivan the Terrible and his son Ivan on November 16, 1581
paintings.why: A Russian tsar cradles his own son, whom he has just struck in a fit of rage, and stares in horror at what he's done. Repin painted the terror and regret on his face so well that it shocked viewers; one even slashed the canvas in 1913 and had to be repaired. It's famous for its raw emotion and for how it shows that power can lead to tragedy.

paintings.t: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
paintings.why: Gauguin painted this huge canvas in Tahiti as a kind of life story, from a baby on the right to an old woman on the left. The title asks three of life's biggest questions. He considered it his masterpiece and said he painted it before planning to end his life, though he lived on. It's famous for its dreamy colors and for asking questions everyone wonders about.

Two women rest in each other's arms on a rumpled bed, caught in a quiet moment. Courbet was a Realist, who wanted to paint life honestly, and the painting was considered scandalous when it was made. Today, it's admired for its soft light and gentle skin tones. It remains an important example of how artists began exploring private moments.

Women in Breton costumes kneel around a bright yellow crucifix in a golden autumn field. Gauguin was inspired by a wooden carving in a village chapel in Brittany, France. He used flat, bold colors and dark outlines instead of realistic shading. It's a landmark of Synthetism, a style that favored feeling and symbol over copying the world.

Purple irises with green leaves grow in a zigzag across a folding screen of glittering gold, with a bridge made of eight planks. Ogata Kōrin painted this around 1710 based on a famous story from The Tales of Ise, a classic Japanese tale. The flat shapes and rich colors are like a beautiful pattern. It's one of the most famous Japanese paintings and a national treasure in Japan.
paintings.k: The irises zigzag across the screen. Can you find the bridge?

paintings.why: Officially titled 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1', this portrait shows Whistler's mother sitting quietly in profile, with a plain wall and a framed print behind her. Whistler cared about shapes and colors, like musical notes, more than about the story. It became a symbol of motherhood and has been parodied for over a century. It's even been called America's most famous painting.

A blazing orange sunset glows over a wild hillside of twisted trees near Arles. For many years, the painting sat forgotten in an attic and was believed to be fake — until 2013, when experts confirmed it as a real Van Gogh. It was a big news story! It's special because it reveals a rare, undiscovered landscape by one of history's most loved artists.

Two women sit on the ground in Tahiti in bright colorful clothes, one gazing out with a serious look. Gauguin moved to the South Pacific hoping to find a simpler world, and his bold colors and flat shapes helped inspire modern art. The title is a question put to a woman by her neighbors. In 2015 it was reported to have sold for around $300 million, among the highest prices ever.

paintings.t: Charles IV of Spain and His Family
paintings.why: Goya painted the royal family of Spain standing in a stiff row, dressed in their grandest clothes. But look closer: the faces look ordinary, even a bit unflattering, and Goya himself is peeking from the back left, just as Velázquez did in 'Las Meninas'. He painted the royals with surprising honesty. It's admired for its sparkling fabrics and for its clever, daring truthfulness.

A farm cart splashes across a shallow stream in front of a cottage, beneath a huge sky of drifting clouds. Constable painted the scene near his boyhood home in Suffolk, England, and it's full of real countryside. When it was shown in Paris in 1824, French artists were amazed by its fresh, natural look. It has become one of the most beloved images of the English countryside.
paintings.k: Find the dog at the edge of the water. Where is the cart going?

paintings.why: An ancient king lounges on a huge bed, calmly watching his palace be destroyed in a whirlwind of red, gold and chaos. Delacroix based it on a poem by Lord Byron. Critics in 1827 thought it was messy and over the top. But its explosion of color and action thrilled other artists, and it became a landmark of the Romantic movement.

paintings.t: Night Rain at Karasaki, from the series Eight Views of Ōmi
paintings.why: A giant, ancient pine tree stands at the edge of Lake Biwa on a rainy night, with the rain pouring down in dark lines. Utagawa Hiroshige made this woodblock print in the 1830s as part of a series of Eight Views of Ōmi. The tree and the soft ink gradations create a moody, magical feel. It's one of his most famous landscapes.

Courbet shows himself painting a landscape in the center of a huge room, surrounded by friends, models, and the poor on the other side. He called it a 'real allegory' of his life as an artist. The huge scale, usually reserved for history paintings, was a bold statement. It's famous for declaring that a painter's own world is worth painting.

A woman and a man sit side by side at a Paris café, yet each seems lost in their own lonely thoughts. Degas placed them off-center and tilted the tables, as if a camera snapped the scene by accident. Viewers in 1876 were not used to such honest, unglamorous pictures. It remains famous for showing the quiet sadness that can exist inside a busy city.

Friends laugh, flirt and share wine on a sunny balcony beside the Seine river. Renoir painted his real friends, and the woman at left holding a little dog became his future wife. Light dances over the tablecloth, the fruit, and everyone's straw hats. It's one of the happiest paintings ever made and is why people still smile when they see it.

Four bear cubs play on a fallen tree in a misty pine forest at dawn. Shishkin painted the trees and Savitsky added the bears, though the museum collector later erased Savitsky's name from the signature! The golden light filtering through the fog makes you feel the cool morning air. It is one of the best-loved paintings in Russia, famous even from candy wrappers.
paintings.k: Count the bear cubs. Which one is climbing and which one is peeking?

paintings.t: A Journalist Lecturing on the Orrery
paintings.why: A lecturer shows a model of the solar system, called an orrery, to a group of people gathered around a lamp that stands for the Sun. Wright painted the awe on their faces as they learn how planets move. The painting celebrated science at a time when new ideas were exciting everyone. It's famous for making learning look as dramatic as an adventure.

A girl in a glowing yellow dress leans on a plump pillow, absorbed in her book. Fragonard painted her with quick, feathery brushwork, almost like he was sketching in paint. It celebrates the quiet pleasure of reading, which still feels familiar today. It's one of the most charming pictures in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

In 1822 Greek islanders suffered a terrible attack during their war for independence, and Delacroix painted the grief and suffering that followed. The painting is full of weary survivors in a sweeping landscape, shown with deep sympathy. French viewers were moved, and it helped build support for the Greek cause. It also made Delacroix a leader of the Romantic movement.

A young woman holds a jar of water that pours into a spring, standing gracefully against a rocky background. Ingres first worked on this for years, and the final version was completed in 1856 with help from his students. It became a symbol of purity and the natural spring of life. It was a hit with the public and remained a favorite of French painting for generations.

An old man sits in a chair with his head buried in his fists, overwhelmed by sorrow. Van Gogh painted it in 1890 from an earlier drawing, near the end of his life, and said he wanted to show deep feelings. The thick, wavy brushstrokes and strong blue make the sadness easy to see. It's powerful because it shows emotion anyone can understand.

A young woman reclines on a green couch in a white gown with a golden sash, gazing out confidently. Goya painted this as a twin to the famous nude version, and each could be switched in a hidden frame. It's famous for its sparkling fabric and for the mystery of who she was. It's still one of the best-loved works in Madrid's Prado Museum.

Ruins of an abbey rise in a misty twilight, with bare oak trees and a quiet funeral procession of monks. Friedrich was interested in mortality and faith, and he painted this gloomy, moving scene when he was in his thirties. It helped make him a star of German Romanticism. It's remembered for its mysterious, hushed mood.

A young couple shares a passionate kiss on a staircase as the man prepares to leave on a journey. Hayez painted it to express the Italian wish for freedom, because it was a time when Italians were fighting for unity. Look at the shimmering blue dress, which became one of the most famous patches of color in Italian art. It's loved as a symbol of love and patriotism.

Dante and the Roman poet Virgil cross a stormy river in the underworld in a little boat while tortured souls cling to the sides. Delacroix was only 24, and this painting launched his career. The dark drama and strong colors were a daring change from the calmer art of the time. It's remembered as the first great Romantic painting.

Great jagged slabs of ice are heaped like a shattered ship against a pale polar sky. Friedrich painted this icy world to show how powerful nature can be, and how small people are. Hidden in the ice is the wreck of a ship, a reminder of human limits. It's one of the great paintings of nature's wild beauty.

As the volcano Vesuvius erupts, the people of ancient Pompeii run in terror under falling stones and lightning. Bryullov spent years researching the real ruins to make it accurate. When it was shown in Italy and Russia, crowds cheered and the writer Pushkin praised it. It's famous for combining drama with real history.

Dozens of women are crowded together in a circular steamy bathhouse in this unusual round painting. Ingres finished it when he was 82, and it's considered a final masterpiece of his career. It was inspired by stories from travelers. The unusual circular shape resembles a view through a keyhole.

Four people stand on a balcony in green shutters, looking out in different directions as if lost in thoughts. Manet was inspired by a painting by Goya, and the flat, bold colors were thought odd in 1869. The figures don't speak to each other, which gives a modern, mysterious feeling. The painter Berthe Morisot, an Impressionist herself, sits in front.

A proud young woman in a dark velvet hat and furs looks down at us from an open carriage on a snowy street. Kramskoi never said who she was, so she's remained a mystery. Her glowing face and confident gaze make her one of the most famous faces in Russian art. People still wonder about her story.

A woman sleeps in the desert under a full moon while a lion sniffs at her and walks away. Rousseau painted it with flat, dreamlike shapes and strange calm. He had no formal training, so his art has a childlike purity. It's famous as a masterpiece of 'naive' art and a forerunner of surrealism.
paintings.k: The full moon is shining. What do you think the lion is going to do?

paintings.t: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
paintings.why: A scientist pumps the air out of a glass jar holding a white cockatoo as the family watches, some fascinated and some upset. Wright painted it by candlelight to build suspense, asking whether science is always right. It's a rare painting that makes a science experiment feel like a thrilling drama. It sits among the most famous works of the Enlightenment.

paintings.t: Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway
paintings.why: A steam train rushes toward us across a bridge through a misty, golden haze of rain and light. Turner painted it when railways were brand-new and thrilling, and he captured the feeling of speed. A tiny hare runs ahead of the engine. It's loved as a glimpse of the modern world arriving.
paintings.k: A train is rushing through the rain. Can you spot the little hare?

paintings.why: Three women bend over in a golden field to gather leftover grain after the harvest, while far behind them workers pile up huge stacks of wheat. Gleaning was the work of the very poor, and Millet gave them heroic, monumental dignity. Some wealthy viewers disliked it, but today it's treasured. It is a landmark of respect for working people.

A stylish Parisian socialite stands in a plunging black dress, her skin pale and her head turned in profile. When Sargent showed it in 1884, people were scandalized — especially because one dress strap had slipped off her shoulder. He repainted it to the right place, but the damage to his Paris career was done. Today it's one of the greatest portraits of elegance and confidence.

In a gothic workshop, an alchemist falls to his knees with astonishment as a strange glow rises in his flask — the discovery of phosphorus, which glows in the dark. Wright painted the pale glow as though it were magic. The picture celebrates the thrill of discovery. It's a marvelous example of dramatic lighting.

In the streets of Madrid, citizens rise up with knives against Napoleon's mounted soldiers. Goya painted this and its companion, 'The Third of May', six years later to honor the people who fought. The chaotic fight swirls with horses and flashing blades. It's a landmark of war painting that focuses on ordinary people.

A crowd of Parisians chat and listen to a concert under tall trees in the Tuileries Garden. Manet painted his friends, including poets, musicians and fellow artists. The faces are dabbed in quickly, which was daring at the time. It's celebrated as one of the first paintings of modern city life in Paris.

paintings.t: Skull of a Skeleton with Burning Cigarette
paintings.why: A skeleton's skull seems to puff on a cigarette in this funny, spooky, and thoughtful painting. Van Gogh was a young art student in Antwerp when he painted it, likely as a student joke. Skulls have long been used in art to remind us that life is short. It's become one of his most reproduced images.

A tall dark cypress tree reaches up between a glowing crescent moon and a bright star, while travelers walk along a winding road below. Van Gogh painted this in 1890, one of his last great paintings. The swirling sky and flame-like tree give a sense of energy. It captures his love of the night.

Two men watch in horror as a demon-like figure bites a man in a fight between damned souls in Hell, taken from Dante's poem. Bouguereau was young when he painted this, and its strong, twisted bodies show his skill. It's less gentle than his famous later works. It's remembered as a dramatic and daring early success.

George Washington stands boldly in a boat full of soldiers crossing an icy river on Christmas night in 1776, before a surprise attack on enemy troops. Leutze painted it in Germany, and it's much larger than a car. Experts note details that aren't accurate, but it became the best-known picture of the American Revolution. It's a classic example of heroic history painting.

A woman lies on her back playing with a parrot perched on her hand, her hair flowing loosely. Courbet painted her with realistic detail, when the Salon expected idealized goddesses. It was both admired and criticized. It became a highlight of the Metropolitan Museum's French collection.

A sunny terrace overlooks a sparkling sea with sailboats, with a family relaxing among bright flowers. Monet painted it when he was 27 at his aunt's home on the Normandy coast. The bold, flat blocks of color show the influence of Japanese prints. It's an early, joyful look at the Impressionist style.

paintings.t: Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son
paintings.why: A woman and a young boy stand on a breezy hilltop, with the sunlit sky behind them. Monet painted his wife Camille and their son Jean out of doors, with fast brushstrokes to catch the wind and light. We see her from below, so she seems to float against the clouds. It's a delight of the Impressionist movement.

A girl on a swing and some friends are caught in dappled sunlight filtering through the trees. Renoir painted blotches of blue shadow on the white dress, which some critics scoffed at as dirty! We now see it as a brilliant study of light. It's one of the happiest Impressionist works.

A quiet bare garden stands in front of a church in the Netherlands, where Van Gogh's father was a pastor. He painted it in earthy, muted tones when he was a young artist, before his famous bright colors. The painting was stolen from a Dutch museum in 2020 and was recovered a few years later. It's a quiet look at his early life.

A kind art-supply dealer sits in front of a wall of Japanese woodblock prints, wearing a straw hat and a calm smile. Père Tanguy supported struggling artists like Van Gogh, who painted him in bright colors. It shows how much Van Gogh admired Japanese art. It's a rare, happy portrait of a good friend.

A little white house glows in the blue dusk with lighted windows, under a dark tree and a deep blue sky. Van Gogh painted this in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise during his final weeks. The warm light pouring from the windows feels like a welcome home. It remains one of his cozy, quiet nighttime scenes.

A young woman in a glowing orange dress is curled up asleep in a sunny courtyard, with the sea behind her. Leighton used the vivid color to suggest the heat of summer. For years the painting was forgotten and even sold cheaply, and then rediscovered. Today it's one of the most loved Victorian paintings, and it now hangs in a museum in Puerto Rico.

Figures arch like a cathedral around a lake, their bodies simplified into solid blocks and triangles of blue and green. Cézanne worked on his big bather paintings for years and left this one near the end of his life. It paved the way for Cubism and modern art. Picasso and Matisse studied it closely.

In a Greek myth, the princess Danaë was shut in a tower and visited by Zeus in a shower of gold. Klimt painted her curled up while the gold rains down. The shimmering patterns and rich colors show his signature style. It's one of the most famous mythological paintings of the early 1900s.

A woman sleeps stretched backward on a bed as a creepy little creature sits on her chest and a horse's head peeks through the curtain. Fuseli's painting was a sensation in London in 1782, because it so vividly shows what it's like to have a bad dream. It's an early classic of the horror genre. It has inspired countless artists.

paintings.t: The Intervention of the Sabine Women
paintings.why: In the legend of ancient Rome, women rush between two armies to stop a battle between their fathers and their husbands. David painted it after the French Revolution as a message of peace and unity. The figures are posed like statues in a clear, bright light. It took him years to complete.

A pale old warship, famous from the Battle of Trafalgar, is towed by a small steam tugboat to be broken up for scrap, while the sun sets in a blaze of gold. Turner showed the end of the age of sail and the start of the steam age. It was voted Britain's favorite painting in a 2005 poll. People still love its feeling of farewell.
paintings.k: A big ship is being towed by a small boat. Which one do you think is doing the hard work?

paintings.why: Women in summery white dresses stroll and gather flowers in a sunny garden. Monet painted it outdoors, even digging a trench so he could reach the top of the huge canvas. The way sunlight filters through the dresses was striking. It was rejected from the 1867 Salon but is now treasured.

A woman stands in the surf as waves roll against a stormy sky. Courbet painted the sea many times and loved its raw power. The painting was shown in Paris in 1868 and was praised for its realism. It captures the thrill of the ocean.

A group of women relax by a stream, painted with soft, sculptural outlines. Renoir spent three years working on it, trying to copy the classic style of Italian masters he'd admired on a trip. Critics weren't sure, because he'd left Impressionism behind. It marks a turning point in his career.

Two women sit on a sandy shore in Tahiti, relaxed and thoughtful, painted in bold, flat colors. Gauguin left France to live in the South Pacific hoping to find an unspoiled way of life. The strong colors and simple shapes were different from European art. It inspired later artists to use color freely.

Two girls in pretty dresses lean over a piano, gently reading music together. Renoir painted several versions of this scene, and the French government bought one for the Musée du Luxembourg. The soft, glowing colors give it a feeling of warmth. It's a gentle portrait of music at home.

In Greek legend, a young man named Hylas goes to fetch water and is enchanted by water nymphs who pull him into their pond. Waterhouse painted the water lilies and glowing faces with great skill. It was displayed in Manchester Art Gallery, which once removed it for a few days in 2018 to spark a conversation. It is still a favorite of fans of myth and magic.

In the Bible, Judith saves her city by defeating an enemy general. Klimt shows her in a shimmering gold collar, with half-closed eyes and a mysterious expression. The glittering patterns are inspired by Egyptian and Byzantine art. It's famous for combining ancient legend with modern, golden style.

A woman sits on a bed seen from behind, her head wrapped in a turban, with silky white sheets and a curtain. Ingres painted this in Rome when he was just 28. Admirers praise the smooth, glowing skin and the elegant curve of her back. It's one of the best-known works of Neoclassical art.

Three people look out between tall white chalk cliffs and a twisted tree frame to the sparkling Baltic Sea. Friedrich painted it after his honeymoon on the island of Rügen, and the figures feel awestruck by the beauty. The hidden details, like the man on his hands and knees looking over the edge, invite you to imagine it yourself. It's among the most famous Romantic landscapes.

This tiny portrait, painted in watercolor on ivory, is about the size of a playing card. Sarah Goodridge was a miniature painter who made it in 1828 as a private gift to a friend. Because it is so small and personal, it's one of the most unusual works in early American art. It's remarkable for showing how a woman artist of the 1820s boldly made her own choices.

Two laborers break stones on a roadside, one old and one young, with faces hidden from view. Courbet saw them at work and invited them to model. Painting poor workers life-size was considered shocking. The original was destroyed in 1945 during World War II, but copies show its impact.

The goddess Venus drifts on the waves, her arm raised over her eyes, while little cupids fly around her. Cabanel's version was shown in 1863, the same year as Manet's scandalous picnic, and the Emperor Napoleon III bought it. It was the toast of the Paris Salon. It shows the polished, perfect style that Impressionists would rebel against.

Well-dressed Parisians stroll across a huge, wet intersection, holding umbrellas, with shiny gray cobblestones and handsome new buildings. Caillebotte painted it to show the modern, rebuilt Paris, which he knew well. The unusual cropping and perspective feel like a photograph. It's one of the best-known pictures of city life.

A crowd of Parisians hurry along a rainy street under a sea of umbrellas. Renoir started this painting in his bright Impressionist style, then changed the figures on the left years later after he'd adopted a sharper, more classical look. That's why two styles live in one painting. It's a delightful picture of a rainy day in the city.

paintings.t: Agostina Segatori Sitting in the Café du Tambourin
paintings.why: A woman sits at a round table in a Paris café, her tambourine-shaped table, and cigarette at hand, in front of a wall covered with Japanese prints. Van Gogh knew her personally; she ran the café. He used bright, flat colors for the first time, after he moved to Paris. It's an early step toward his famous style.

An elderly man in colorful robes plays a flute, hoping to teach a group of tortoises. They creep along with little interest. Osman Hamdi Bey's painting is thought by many to be a gentle joke about how slowly people accept change. It's the most famous painting from Turkey and sold for a record price in 2004.
paintings.k: How many tortoises can you count? Are they listening?

paintings.why: A young landowner and his wife pose proudly in their own fields in Suffolk, England, as if showing off their land. Gainsborough painted this when he was only 21, and it features crops and sheep as well as the couple. It is one of the most famous English portraits. It's also a record of how people showed off their wealth.

A woman in a dark landscape raises her hands in grief. Wright of Derby painted this from a poem about a woman mourning her husband. The moonlit night and dramatic lighting make the scene feel eerie. It's a haunting example of the artist's skill with light.

A tiny figure stands on a deserted beach before a huge, empty sea and stormy sky. Friedrich originally painted a few boats but covered them up, leaving only sea, sky, and a lone person. The emptiness felt shocking and modern; a German writer said it was like having your eyelids cut off! It's now seen as a masterpiece about being alone with nature.

A fallen angel with a tormented expression sits alone on a rocky peak with his head in his hands. Cabanel painted it in 1847, inspired by Milton's poem Paradise Lost. The painting shows both beauty and sorrow. It's a classic of the French Academy.

paintings.t: The Meeting, or Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet!
paintings.why: Courbet, with a walking stick and pack, is greeted by his wealthy patron, who bows to him — and the artist stands tall in the sun. The painting is a joke and a statement: a painter who thinks highly of himself. It was shown with a funny title in 1855. It's an iconic portrait of artistic confidence.

Degas painted his aunt's family in Florence: a stern mother in black, a father with his back turned, and two girls. The stiff arrangement suggests the tension in the household. Degas was in his twenties, and this big portrait showed his incredible eye for character. It's now in the Musée d'Orsay.

A man and woman pause in a field at dusk, heads bowed in prayer when the church bell rings. Millet said he was inspired by childhood memories of his grandmother stopping the farm work to pray. It sold for a huge price and became one of the most reproduced images in the world. It's a calm picture of ordinary devotion.

A court jester in red sits alone and gloomy at a party while his king dances in the background. Stańczyk was a real Polish jester known for his wisdom. News has just arrived of a lost city, and he is the only one who sees the danger. The painting shows that the person who jokes may also be the one who worries the most.

A young musician in a red-striped uniform stands against a plain light-gray background, playing his fife. Manet was inspired by Japanese prints and Velázquez in making the figure flat and bold. The Salon rejected it in 1866, and critics said it looked like a playing card. Today we cherish its simplicity and punch.

A solitary figure sits on a rock at dawn, wrestling with a hard decision, as described in the Bible. Kramskoi painted Jesus as a tired, thoughtful man, not a glowing saint. The grey and blue colors set a quiet mood. It's regarded as one of the great Russian religious paintings.

A woman and a small girl in front of a iron fence, with clouds of steam rising behind them from a train in a station. Manet painted it near the Gare Saint-Lazare in Paris. Neither of the figures looks at the train, which was unusual for such a subject. It's a snapshot of modern life with steam and iron.

A stylish couple sits in a theater box, but the woman in her striped gown is looking out at the audience while the man peers up through binoculars. Renoir painted it in 1874 and showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition. It sparkles with black, white and pearly pink. It's loved for its elegance and its sense of being seen.

In 1410 the armies of Poland and Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Knights in one of the largest battles of medieval Europe. Matejko painted it nearly as big as a wall, with hundreds of soldiers in a swirling clash. Poland was not an independent nation when he painted it, so the picture inspired national pride. It remains Poland's most famous painting.

A glowing moon shines over a calm river and a few small huts, with a path of silvery light across the water. Kuindzhi hid lamps behind his canvases when showing them to make the moonlight seem almost real. In 1880 crowds lined up in the dark to look at it. It's still known for its magic glow.

Two girls in fancy hats and dresses sit on a terrace beside the Seine in Chatou, one holding a ball of wool. Renoir loved painting young people, and this one glows with soft red and green. It's also known as 'On the Terrace.' It was one of his big successes.

A young woman with glowing skin lifts her arms as the morning sun rises behind her, with the pale light of day. Bouguereau often painted allegories, scenes that represent ideas — here, the beginning of the day. He was a master of smooth, polished surfaces. The painting delighted viewers at the Paris Salon.

Young working-class men relax and bathe along the Seine, with factory chimneys in the distance. Seurat painted it in his careful, smooth style, and the stillness feels like time has stopped. It was his first big painting, and it was turned down by the Salon. It's now admired as a calm, quiet and modern masterpiece.

Two little girls light paper lanterns at dusk, surrounded by tall lilies and roses. Sargent painted for months, working only for a few minutes each evening when the light was right. The title comes from a popular song of the time. It's one of the most magical pictures of twilight.

The ancient Roman emperor Heliogabalus is said to have thrown a party where guests were buried beneath a flood of rose petals. Alma-Tadema painted the shower of pink petals falling over the cheerful and doomed party. He studied roses so he could paint them in the correct season. It's celebrated for showing Rome as a world of luxury and drama.

A thin, tired man walks into a room — he's a returning exile, and his family stares in stunned surprise. Repin painted the faces so carefully that each one tells a story. The picture asks viewers to imagine what happens next. It's one of the best-loved Russian paintings.

In a poem by Tennyson, a lady who lives in a tower is cursed to never look out directly, but she does, and sails to Camelot in a boat. Waterhouse shows her drifting in her boat, with candles flickering out. It's one of the most popular paintings in the Tate Britain. People love its mix of beauty and sadness.
paintings.k: She floats in a boat with candles flickering. How many candles can you see?

paintings.why: Van Gogh looks out with intense green-blue eyes against a background of swirling blue waves, wearing a blue coat. He painted several self-portraits, partly because he could not afford models. This one was made in 1889 after leaving hospital. It's one of the best-known self-portraits in the world.

Delicate white and pink flowers branch out against a pale blue sky. Van Gogh painted it for his new nephew, named after him, born to his brother Theo in 1890. The branches are painted large, like in Japanese prints. It's one of his most tender and joyful paintings.

In the Greek myth, a vain young man falls in love with his own reflection, while the nymph Echo watches heartbroken. Waterhouse painted the dreamy, mossy pool in lovely detail. It's the origin of the words 'narcissist' and 'echo.' The painting is celebrated for bringing myth to life.

A knight in armor rides calmly through a dark valley while Death with an hourglass and a horned Devil follow behind him. Albrecht Dürer made this engraving in 1513, and its themes of death and courage echo the fears of the plague years.

paintings.t: Napoleon I on his Imperial Throne
paintings.why: Napoleon sits like a god on a golden throne, with the crown of laurel leaves and a scepter, in a gleaming robe. Ingres painted him in 1806, imitating old religious pictures of Jupiter and of kings. The detail of the fabric, gold and fur is extraordinary. It's a spectacular example of power portraiture.

A blind girl sits at the roadside with her sister after a rainstorm, a double rainbow in the sky — which she cannot see. Millais painted it from the real countryside near Winchelsea in England, with its glowing, wet colors. She feels the warm sun and touches the grass. The painting makes us think about everything we notice and everything we miss.

Two women in fancy dresses rest in the grass beside a river, one lying down and one sitting up with a hat. Courbet painted real contemporary women, not goddesses, which angered the critics of 1857. The painting is bold in its color and sense of ordinary leisure. It's seen as a step toward Impressionism.

A young woman is being sold at an oriental slave market and is displayed to buyers. Gérôme painted many scenes of the Middle East that he imagined from travel, and this painting shows a cruel practice. Today the artwork is mainly valued as a record of how Europeans looked at the world, and for what it teaches about the injustice of slavery. It's studied as much for history as for art.

In an ancient Roman arena, a victorious gladiator awaits the crowd's verdict — thumbs down, which meant show no mercy. Gérôme studied Roman history to get details right. The scene has inspired countless films about gladiators. It's one of the most famous images of ancient Rome.

paintings.t: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses
paintings.why: The enchantress Circe holds out a magic cup to Ulysses, hoping to turn him into an animal, as she did to his crew. A mirror behind her shows the hero, alert and holding his sword. Waterhouse painted rich fabrics and a hall of green. It's a thrilling moment from Homer's Odyssey.

A woman reclines on a red cushion, painted with warm colors and Modigliani's smooth, simplified shapes. It was shown in 1917, and the police closed the exhibition because of it. The painting later sold for more than $150 million in 2015. It's one of the most valuable paintings of the 20th century.

paintings.t: Romeo and Juliet: the Tomb Scene
paintings.why: Romeo has taken poison, and Juliet is waking up in the crypt, with a lamp casting a dramatic glow. Wright of Derby painted several scenes from Shakespeare's plays. His use of dark and light heightens the tragedy. It's a moving take on one of the greatest love stories.

A white-bearded figure leans out of a glowing orb in the sky, stretching down a giant pair of compasses to measure and create the world. Blake made this as a print and painted it by hand, and he reportedly worked on it near the end of his life. It shows God as a great designer, but also a bit scary. It's one of the most famous images of creation in art.

paintings.t: The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries
paintings.why: Napoleon stands in his study at night in his general's uniform, his candles nearly burnt down and the clock showing about 4 a.m. David wanted to show him as a leader who works through the night for his people. The details, like the sword and the folded paper, were carefully chosen. It's among the most famous portraits of Napoleon.

Only the head of a small dog peeks out at the bottom of a huge empty golden-brown space. Goya painted it on a wall of his house when he was an old man. Nobody knows what he meant, so people have been wondering ever since. Many see it as a quiet, powerful picture of feeling small and alone.

Women relax in a richly decorated room in Algiers, with patterned fabrics and soft light. Delacroix visited North Africa in 1832 and made quick sketches, then painted this from memory. The bold colors and dazzling light influenced later artists like Renoir, Matisse and Picasso. It's a landmark of color.

Five figures stand on a beach at sunset as five ships sail along the horizon. They stand for different stages of life, from a child to an old man. Friedrich painted this late in his life. Its quiet mood makes people think about the passing of time.

paintings.t: Christ in the House of His Parents
paintings.why: A young Jesus in a carpenter's workshop has hurt his hand on a nail, and his family gathers around him. Millais painted every shaving, tool and detail with scientific care, and the scene hints at future events. When it was shown in 1850, some critics, including Charles Dickens, hated it. Now it's treasured as a daring early Pre-Raphaelite painting.

A woman kneels to sift grain in a barn while her brother and a younger sibling work beside her. Courbet painted ordinary farm work in warm golden tones, in a large canvas that usually would have been reserved for gods. It was part of his movement to paint real life. It shows the dignity of everyday jobs.

In ancient Greece, the clever lawyer Hypereides defended the famous Phryne in a court. To win the case, he dramatically revealed her to the judges, who were so struck that they let her go. Gérôme made this a scene of high drama. It's remembered as a study of beauty and justice.

A young woman in a straw hat leans against a tree, wrapped in a warm, hazy summer light. Renoir painted this when he was 27, still finding his style. The modeled flesh and dappled leaves are a early taste of his later work. It's a pleasant picture of summer relaxation.

A magpie perches on a gate in a quiet field of dazzling snow, with a small house in the background. Monet painted the shadows in blues and lilacs instead of gray, which was radical in 1869. It's one of the loveliest snow scenes in art. The tiny black-and-white bird gives it humor and rhythm.

Three men kneel on the floor of an apartment to scrape and plane a wooden floor, their bare backs gleaming. Caillebotte painted the workers with the same care as a rich family. This was rare and a bit shocking in 1875. It's famous for its dramatic perspective and its respect for labor.

A woman in a corset and petticoat is at her mirror, powdering her face as a gentleman in a top hat waits on a sofa. Manet painted this just before Émile Zola's novel of the same name was published. The Salon of 1877 rejected it. It is a bold picture of Parisian life, with a bright, glowing white and blue palette.

A girl sits at a table in a sunny dining room, peaches and a knife in front of her and light dancing on her face. Serov painted twelve-year-old Vera Mamontova at her family's country home, working for weeks on the portrait. The fresh, natural light was a joy after stiff, formal portraits. It's one of Russia's best-loved paintings.
paintings.k: How many peaches are on the table? What else can you spot?

paintings.why: Breton women in white caps imagine a scene from the Bible — Jacob wrestling an angel — after hearing a sermon. Gauguin painted the vision with a solid red field and no realistic depth, to show it's a dream. The tree slices across the canvas like a Japanese print. It's a key early work of modern, symbolic art.

A simple wooden chair with a pipe and tobacco sits on a tiled floor. Van Gogh painted it as a companion to a picture of Gauguin's much fancier chair. The ordinary chair in sunlight stands for the artist himself. It's one of the most famous portraits of a person who isn't there.

A circus rider leaps off a galloping white horse, a ringmaster cracks his whip and a clown tumbles. Seurat's last painting is made of tiny dots, with swirling lines to suggest motion. He died before he finished it, in 1891. It remains a lively picture of a night out.
paintings.k: Find the clown, the ringmaster and the rider on the white horse. What tricks do you think they will do next?
